01.note: Four Sages entered the 'orchard', the realm of the Torah's loftiest secrets: Ben Azzai, ben Zoma, Aher, and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva warned the others that when they reached stones of pure marble they must not cry 'Water, water', because one who speaks falsehood will not stand before God. Ben Azzai glimpsed and died; ben Zoma glimpsed and was harmed; Aher 'chopped down the shoots', meaning he became a heretic. Only Rabbi Akiva came out safely.
01.why: The Gemara has been telling how Sages expounded the Divine Chariot and were rewarded; this account shows the danger of the same pursuit, and the Gemara goes on to tell more about ben Zoma and Aher.

people.name: Ben Azzai
people.about: One of the four who entered the orchard; he glimpsed and died.

people.name: Ben Zoma
people.about: One of the four; he glimpsed and was harmed, which the translation explains as losing his mind.

people.name: Aher
people.about: 'The other', the name given to Elisha ben Avuya; one of the four, he became a heretic.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The senior of the four, who warned the others; the only one who came out safely.

terms.meaning: A figure of speech for the deepest mystical secrets of the Torah, entered in mind or vision.
A figure of speech for becoming a heretic, ruining what had been planted.

02.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya was standing on a step on the Temple Mount when ben Zoma saw him and did not stand up for him. Rabbi Yehoshua asked where his thoughts were. Ben Zoma said he had been gazing at the gap between the upper waters and the lower waters, only three fingers wide, citing the verse about God's spirit hovering over the waters like a dove over its young without touching them. Rabbi Yehoshua told his students: 'Ben Zoma is still outside.'
02.why: The Gemara has just said ben Zoma glimpsed the divine and was harmed; this incident is brought about his fate. Afterwards the Gemara itself questions his proof, since the hovering verse comes on the first day and the waters were divided on the second.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage with students, standing on the Temple Mount, whom ben Zoma failed to honor.

people.name: Ben Zoma
people.about: A Sage lost in thought about the mysteries of Creation.

terms.meaning: In Genesis, God divides the waters above the sky from the waters below; ben Zoma was contemplating the space between them.
Not yet inside the secret, that is, he had not yet grasped these matters fully.

03.note: Aher saw the angel Mitatron, who had been permitted to sit and write down Israel's merits. Since he had a tradition that no one sits in heaven, he said: perhaps, Heaven forbid, there are two powers. Mitatron was taken out and struck with sixty rods of fire, asked why he had not stood up when he saw Aher, and given permission to erase Aher's merits. A Divine Voice proclaimed: 'Return, rebellious children', except Aher. Aher said that since he was banished from that world, he would enjoy this one. He solicited a prostitute; she asked if he was not Elisha ben Avuya. He uprooted a radish on Shabbat and gave it to her, and she said: 'He is other.'
03.why: The Gemara has just said that Aher 'chopped down the shoots', becoming a heretic, and asks what led him there; this is its answer. Afterwards it turns to his exchanges with Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Aher
people.about: 'The other': Elisha ben Avuya, a Sage who became a heretic; the prostitute's words give him the name.

people.name: Mitatron
people.about: An angel permitted to sit in heaven and write Israel's merits.

terms.meaning: The heretical idea that some power other than God rules the world.
A voice from heaven announcing God's will.
The Sabbath, on which uprooting a plant is forbidden; Aher did it openly to show he had abandoned the Torah.

04.note: After Aher had gone astray he asked Rabbi Meir about a verse comparing wisdom to gold and glass. Rabbi Meir said words of Torah are as hard to acquire as gold and as easy to lose as glass. Aher answered that Rabbi Akiva, Meir's teacher, had read it differently: broken gold and glass vessels can be repaired, so a Torah scholar who has sinned can be repaired too. Rabbi Meir said: then you too, return. Aher said he had already heard from behind the heavenly curtain: 'Return, rebellious children', except Aher.
04.why: The Gemara is gathering exchanges between Aher and his student Rabbi Meir after Aher went astray; this follows one on another verse, and the refusal it ends with returns in the next story, on the Shabbat ride.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Elisha ben Avuya, a Sage who had gone astray, still teaching Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Aher's student, who urges him to repent.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Meir's teacher, whose reading of the verse Aher quotes.

terms.meaning: The curtain that hides God from the world; to hear something there is to hear a heavenly decree.

05.note: Aher was riding a horse on Shabbat while Rabbi Meir walked behind him to learn Torah. Aher told him to turn back, as by his horse's steps they had reached the Shabbat boundary. Meir said: you too, return. Aher said he had heard behind the curtain that he alone was excluded. Meir took hold of him and brought him to a study hall, where Aher asked a child to recite his verse; the verse was about the wicked. So it went in thirteen synagogues. The last child, who stuttered, seemed to say 'And to Elisha God says, what is it for you to declare My statutes'. Some say Aher had a knife and tore the child apart; others say he said that had he a knife, he would have torn him apart.
05.why: The Gemara is collecting traditions about Aher after he went astray, each turning on his claim that he alone was barred from repentance; it goes on to tell what became of him after death.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Elisha ben Avuya, a Sage turned heretic, who still taught Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Aher's student, who tried to bring him back.

terms.meaning: The distance, about two thousand cubits beyond a town, that one may walk on the Sabbath.
Asking a schoolchild what verse he had just learned, and taking the answer as a sign from heaven.

06.note: When Aher died, it was said he would be neither judged, because he had studied Torah, nor brought into the World-to-Come, because he had sinned. Rabbi Meir said it was better that he be judged and then brought in, and that when he himself died he would make smoke rise from Aher's grave. When Rabbi Meir died, smoke rose from the grave. Rabbi Yohanan asked whether it was a mighty deed to burn one's teacher, and whether no one could save him; he said that when he died he would put out the smoke. When Rabbi Yohanan died, the smoke stopped, and a eulogizer said: 'Even the guard at the entrance could not stand before you, our rabbi.'
06.why: The Gemara has told how Aher was barred from repentance in his lifetime; this tells his fate after death. Next it asks how Rabbi Meir could have learned Torah from him at all.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Elisha ben Avuya, a Torah scholar who sinned and became a heretic.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Aher's student, who arranged for him to be judged.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A later Sage who vowed to rescue Aher and, at his death, did.

terms.meaning: The life after death in which the righteous are rewarded.
A sign that the dead man was being judged and punished, as a step before he could enter the World-to-Come.

07.note: Aher's daughter came to Rabbi and asked him to support her. When she said whose daughter she was, he asked whether any of Aher's offspring were still in the world, quoting a verse that the wicked leave no son or grandson. She said: remember his Torah, not his deeds. At once fire came down and licked Rabbi's bench. Rabbi wept and said that if this is how God protects those who treat the Torah with contempt, how much more so those who honor it.
07.why: The Gemara is completing its account of Aher; her plea to remember his Torah leads into its next question, how Rabbi Meir could learn Torah from such a man, which it answers that one may take the words of a flawed Sage.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the leading Sage, to whom Aher's daughter came for support.

people.name: The daughter of Aher
people.about: Aher's daughter, in need of food, who pleads for her father's memory.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Her father, Elisha ben Avuya, a Torah scholar who became a heretic.

terms.meaning: Used alone, the title refers to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

08.note: Rabba bar Sheila met Elijah the prophet and asked what God was doing. Elijah said God was repeating teachings in the name of all the Sages, but not in Rabbi Meir's name, because Meir had learned from Aher. Rabba bar Sheila objected: Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the inside and threw away the peel. Elijah replied that now God was saying: 'My son Meir says: when a person suffers, the Divine Presence says, My head is heavy, My arm is heavy. If God grieves so over the blood of the wicked, how much more over the blood of the righteous.'
08.why: The Gemara has been asking how Rabbi Meir could learn Torah from Aher and answering that a scholar can take the good and leave the rest, like a date or a nut; this story shows heaven accepting that defense.

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: A Sage who met Elijah and defended Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who reports to Rabba bar Sheila what God is doing.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who learned from Aher; God at first will not quote him.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, pictured studying and quoting the teachings of the Sages.

terms.meaning: God's presence in the world, the Shekhina, here pictured as feeling a sufferer's pain.
Rulings of Jewish law.

09.note: Yehuda ben Tabbai had a false witness executed, to counter the Sadducees, who held such witnesses are executed only if their victim was executed. Shimon ben Shatah told him he had shed innocent blood, since the Sages taught that false witnesses are executed only when both are proven false. At once Yehuda ben Tabbai resolved never to rule on law except in Shimon ben Shatah's presence. All his life he lay on the executed man's grave, and his voice could be heard. People thought it was the dead man's voice. He said it was his own, and that they would know it when he died, for then the voice would no longer be heard.
09.why: The mishna lists the pairs of Sages who led the Sanhedrin, and Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree over which of these two was the head; the Gemara asks which view this account follows, since it has Yehuda ben Tabbai ruling in front of Shimon ben Shatah.

people.name: Yehuda ben Tabbai
people.about: A Sage who had a false witness executed and spent his life in penance for it.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: His colleague, who told him he had shed innocent blood.

terms.meaning: A witness proven to have given false testimony to harm someone; the Torah gives him the penalty he tried to bring on his victim.
A Jewish group of the Second Temple period that rejected many traditions of the Sages.
A form of oath: may I not see Israel's consolation if what I say is not true.

10.note: Alexa died in Lod, and all of Israel gathered to eulogize him. Rabbi Tarfon would not let them, because it was the Festival of Shavuot. The text tells nothing more about Alexa or the funeral.
10.why: The mishna allowed eulogies and fasts on the day after Shavuot to reject the Sadducee view that Shavuot always falls on a Sunday; this incident seems to contradict it. The Gemara reads it as the day after the Festival, and says that day is festive only when Shavuot does not fall on Shabbat.

people.name: Alexa
people.about: A man who died in Lod, whom all Israel came to eulogize.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who forbade the eulogy because of the Festival.

terms.meaning: The Festival of Weeks, one of the three pilgrimage festivals, fifty days after Passover.
To mourn the dead publicly with a funeral speech, which is not done on a festival.

10.flag: The story is a single sentence, quoted inside a legal objection; it has an event but almost no narrative.

11.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok told of two women, both married to men who kept the purity laws strictly, whose clothes were switched at the bathhouse. The case came before Rabbi Akiva, and he declared the clothes impure.
11.why: Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram has just ruled that clothes become impure if their owner wore them mistaking them for others, because his attention lapsed; this incident supports him. Rabbi Oshaya then objects that by that logic any mix-up would make food impure.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who ruled the switched clothes impure.

terms.meaning: 'Associates': people committed to keeping the laws of ritual purity strictly, even for ordinary food.
Ritually impure: unfit for contact with pure food or holy things until purified. It is a religious status, not dirt.

12.note: A woman came to Rabbi Yishmael and said she had woven a garment while ritually pure, though she had not set her mind on keeping it pure. As he questioned her, she mentioned that a menstruating woman had pulled the rope with her. Rabbi Yishmael said: how great are the words of the Sages, who said that if one's mind is on guarding an item, it is pure, and if not, it is impure.
12.why: The Gemara is challenging rulings that clothes become impure when their owner mistakes them for others; Rabba bar Avuh raises this case to show that what counts is whether one meant to guard the item, not whether one knew what it was.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage to whom a woman brought a question about her weaving.

terms.meaning: Under the purity laws a woman during her period is ritually impure and can make things she moves impure.
Fit for contact with pure food or holy things; a religious status, not cleanliness.

13.note: Another woman came to Rabbi Yishmael and said she had woven a cloth while ritually pure, though she had not set her mind on guarding it. As he questioned her, she said a thread had snapped and she had tied it with her mouth. Rabbi Yishmael said: how great are the words of the Sages, who said that if one's mind is on guarding an item, it is pure, and if not, it is impure.
13.why: This is the second of the cases Rabba bar Avuh raises against the rulings on switched clothes. The Gemara then reconciles Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's case: each wife assumed the other was married to an unlearned man and stopped guarding her clothes.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage to whom a woman brought a question about her weaving.

terms.meaning: Saliva wet the thread; under the purity laws a liquid readily takes on impurity and passes it to the cloth.

14.note: Rabbi Yehoshua said he was ashamed of Beit Shammai's ruling: could a woman and her bowl be impure for seven days while the dough she kneads in it stays pure? A student of Beit Shammai offered to explain. He got Rabbi Yehoshua to agree that an impure vessel does not block impurity and that an unlearned man's vessel is impure, then said: if you tell such a man his vessel is impure, will he listen? He will say, 'Mine is pure and yours is impure.' At once Rabbi Yehoshua went and lay on the graves of Beit Shammai and said: 'I humble myself before you, bones of Beit Shammai.' It was said that all his life his teeth were dark from his fasts.
14.why: The mishna records Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel arguing over what stays pure in a room with a corpse; this story gives Beit Shammai's reasoning, from which the Gemara concludes that the purity of the unlearned man's vessels matters to the observant as well.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who mocked Beit Shammai's ruling and then did penance for it.

people.name: A student of Beit Shammai
people.about: An unnamed student who explained the school's reasoning to Rabbi Yehoshua.

terms.meaning: The school of the Sage Shammai, whose rulings often differ from those of the school of Hillel.
Literally 'people of the land': someone who does not keep the purity laws carefully, so his things are treated as impure.
The impurity a corpse passes on, which takes a week-long purification.
A sealed vessel that stops corpse impurity spreading to what is beyond it.

15.note: A man was carrying a barrel of sacrificial wine from place to place. The strap of his sandal, which had become impure from being trodden on by a zav, broke off. He picked it up and laid it on the mouth of the barrel; it fell into the barrel's airspace and made the wine impure. At that time the Sages declared that one carrying an object trodden by a zav may carry teruma with it, but not sacrificial food.
15.why: The mishna allows carrying teruma, but not sacrificial food, alongside an object trodden by a zav, and the Gemara asks why sacrificial food is different; this incident is the answer. It then asks why the rule was not extended to teruma.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rav Yehuda reports the incident.

terms.meaning: A man with a certain bodily discharge; he is ritually impure, and anything he treads or sits on becomes impure too.
The portion of produce given to priests; holy, but less so than food from Temple offerings.
Food from Temple offerings, which has the strictest purity rules.
An earthenware vessel becomes impure when an impure thing enters the space inside it, even without touching its contents.

16.note: A man was carrying the water and ashes used for purification across the Jordan in a boat. An olive-sized piece of a corpse was then found stuck in the floor of the boat. At that time the Sages declared that no one may carry the water and ashes of purification across the Jordan in a boat.
16.why: Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya held that a decree prompted by an incident covers only that incident's exact circumstances, the Jordan and a boat; this is that incident. The Gemara uses his view to explain why the sandal decree applies to sacrificial food and not teruma.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rav Yehuda reports the incident.

terms.meaning: Water mixed with ashes of the red heifer, sprinkled to purify people and things impure from contact with the dead.
A piece the size of an olive, the smallest amount of a corpse that makes things impure.

17.note: Rabbi Abba was standing before Rav Huna when Rav Huna heard a woman say God's name in vain. He ostracized her, and then at once released her from it, in her presence.
17.why: Rav has just ruled that one who hears God's name said in vain must ostracize the speaker, and that a ban imposed in someone's presence is lifted only in their presence; the Gemara draws both rulings from this incident, and a third: the ban can be lifted at once.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The Sage who saw what happened and reports it.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who ostracized a woman for saying God's name in vain.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban (niddui), a formal shunning by the community, which a Sage can impose and lift.
Saying the divine name for no purpose, such as in a needless oath.

18.note: Shimon HaTzaddik said that as a priest he ate the guilt-offering of an impure nazirite only once. A nazirite came from the South with beautiful eyes, a handsome face and curled hair, and Shimon asked why he would destroy such hair. The man said he had been a shepherd for his father; drawing water from a spring, he saw his reflection and his evil inclination rose up and sought to drive him from the world. He told himself: 'Wicked one, why are you proud of what will be food for worms? I swear I will shave you for Heaven.' Shimon HaTzaddik rose, kissed his head, and said: may there be more nazirites like you in Israel.
18.why: Rabbi Meir has said it is good to take a nazirite vow, and the Gemara asks why, given the risk of failing to keep it; the answer is that he follows Shimon HaTzaddik, who praised this nazirite's vow because it was made for Heaven.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: A priest, 'the Righteous', who tells the story.

people.name: The nazirite from the South
people.about: A handsome young shepherd who took a nazirite vow to master his pride.

terms.meaning: Someone who vows for a time to avoid wine, haircuts and contact with the dead, and shaves his head at the end.
A sacrifice brought by a nazirite who became impure, after which he shaves and starts his term over; priests eat from it.
The urge within a person toward sin.

19.note: Imma Shalom, wife of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, was asked why her children were so beautiful. She said her husband was intimate with her only at midnight, and that when he 'converses' with her (the text's word) he uncovers a handbreadth and covers a handbreadth, like a man compelled by a demon. When she asked him why, he said it was so that he would not set his eyes on another woman, which would bring his children close to the status of mamzerim.
19.why: Rabbi Yohanan ben Dehavai has just said deaf children come from parents who talk during intercourse; the Gemara sets Imma Shalom's account of a Sage who did talk against it, and answers that talk about intimacy itself is allowed.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: The wife of Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, asked why her children were so beautiful.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus
people.about: Her husband, a Sage, who explains his conduct to her.

terms.meaning: A child born of a forbidden union such as adultery; here a figure for the harm of a man thinking of another woman.
A measure about the width of a hand.

20.note: Ulla was travelling up to the Land of Israel when two men from Hozai joined him. One rose and slaughtered the other, then asked Ulla: 'Did I do right?' Ulla said: 'Yes, and open the place of the slaughter.' When Ulla came before Rabbi Yohanan he asked whether, Heaven forbid, he had strengthened the hands of sinners. Rabbi Yohanan said: 'You saved your life.'
20.why: The Gemara has been warning against anger, citing the curse of 'a trembling heart'. Afterwards Rabbi Yohanan asks how such rage arose on the way to the Land of Israel, when that verse speaks of exile; Ulla answers they had not yet crossed the Jordan.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage travelling to the Land of Israel who witnessed a killing.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage Ulla asked about what he had said to the killer.

terms.meaning: A place in Babylonia that the two travellers came from.
Encouraged someone in doing wrong.
